entity_title: EU registration certificate required after 3 months
fact_text: An EU/EEA citizen may enter and stay in Slovenia for up to three months on an ID card or passport alone, but for any longer stay must obtain a residence registration certificate (potrdilo o prijavi prebivanja) from the local administrative unit (upravna enota) before the three-month period expires. This is a registration certificate, not a residence permit.
evidence_quote: For a longer stay, EU citizens must obtain a residence registration certificate at the administrative unit in their area of residence before the expiry of the authorised three-month stay.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Free movement is assumed to mean no paperwork; in fact an EU/EEA professional staying past 90 days must actively register at the upravna enota and receives a certificate, not a permit. Action: book the upravna enota appointment before day 90.

entity_title: Registration certificate is capped at 5 years
fact_text: The residence registration certificate issued to EU/EEA citizens is not open-ended: it is granted for the duration of the intended stay, up to a maximum of five years, and must then be renewed.
evidence_quote: The residence registration certificate is issued to EU citizens for the duration of their intended stay, or for a maximum period of five years.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: EU residence rights feel permanent, but the Slovenian certificate carries a hard five-year cap and lapses if not renewed. Action: diarise the expiry date and renew at the upravna enota before it lapses.

entity_title: Fined but not expelled for failing to register
fact_text: Registering residence after three months is mandatory and the registration certificate confirms the right to live in the country; failing to register can attract a fine, but an EU/EEA citizen cannot be expelled merely for not registering.
evidence_quote: If you are required to register, you may be fined for not doing so but may continue to live in the country and cannot be expelled just for this.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Registration is sometimes treated as optional admin; it is legally required and fineable, yet non-registration never costs the residence right itself. Action: register on time to avoid the fine, but know late registration is not a loss of status.

entity_title: Register your address within 8 days of moving in
fact_text: Registering a Slovenian home address (prijava prebivalisca) in the population register is a separate act from obtaining the residence certificate: temporary residence must be registered with the administrative unit within eight days of taking up that residence.
evidence_quote: Temporary residence must be registered within eight days of the day of taking up temporary residence.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: The population-register address registration is distinct from the EU residence certificate and runs on its own 8-day clock. Action: register the address within 8 days of moving in, in addition to obtaining the residence certificate.

entity_title: Address registration lapses after up to 2 years
fact_text: A registered temporary residence in Slovenia is time-limited: it is recorded for up to two years (or the shorter validity of the underlying certificate, permit or long-stay visa), after which it must be renewed.
evidence_quote: Temporary residence is registered for a period of up to two years or for the period of validity of the temporary residence permit, residence registration certificate or long-stay visa if this is shorter than two years.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Registering an address once is not permanent; the temporary-residence record expires after up to two years. Action: track the address-registration expiry separately from the residence certificate and renew before it lapses.

entity_title: Get a davcna stevilka before your first pay
fact_text: A Slovenian tax number (davcna stevilka) from the Financial Administration (FURS) is a prerequisite for being paid: a first-time arrival must file the DR-02 entry in the tax register before receiving any taxable income or acquiring taxable property.
evidence_quote: First-time comers to Slovenia must submit an application for the entry of natural persons in the tax register (DR-02 form) before their first receipt of taxable income or before first acquisition of taxable movable and immovable property, on the basis of which they will be assigned a Slovenian tax identification number (for the purposes of receiving income in Slovenia).

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Payroll, a bank account and a rental all need the davcna stevilka, and it must exist before the first paycheck. Action: obtain the tax number (DR-02 at FURS) as one of the first steps on arrival, ahead of payroll setup.

entity_title: Report address or bank changes to FURS within 8 days
fact_text: After entry in the tax register, the individual has an ongoing duty to notify FURS of any change to the registered data - for example a new address or bank account - within eight days of the change.
evidence_quote: In case of changing data or additional new data (eg. new address, bank account) persons shall report to the tax authority any change of data from the application within eight days after the occurrence of changes.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: The tax-register record is not set-and-forget; moving flat or switching banks triggers an 8-day reporting duty to FURS. Action: update FURS within 8 days whenever the employee's address or bank account changes.

entity_title: EMSO is a separate ID from the tax number
fact_text: Slovenia uses a 13-digit unique personal number, the EMSO, distinct from the tax number; it is assigned to a foreigner only when they exercise rights or obligations in Slovenia, and the Ministry of the Interior issues it within three working days of a complete application.
evidence_quote: Foreigners are only assigned an EMŠO if they exercise their rights and obligations in the Republic of Slovenia.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Newcomers conflate the EMSO (population-register ID) with the davcna stevilka (tax ID); they are two different numbers from two different authorities and both are needed. Action: expect to obtain both - EMSO via residence registration, tax number via FURS.

entity_title: How Slovenia decides you are tax-resident
fact_text: An EU/EEA professional becomes a Slovenian tax resident on establishing a residential link with Slovenia - such as permanent residence, family living there, or being present more than 183 days in a calendar year - not merely by taking a job there.
evidence_quote: When a person moves or returns to Slovenia (for reasons of employment, study, retirement, etc.) and newly establishes or re-establishes a residential link with Slovenia (such as permanent residence, family living in Slovenia, staying in Slovenia for more than 183 days in a calendar year, etc.), that person becomes a resident for tax purposes.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Tax residency turns on residential ties and the 183-day count, so a short assignment may stay non-resident while a longer one flips to resident mid-year. Action: assess the 183-day and centre-of-interests tests before assuming the employee's tax status.

entity_title: Residents are taxed on worldwide income
fact_text: Once resident for tax purposes, an individual is liable to Slovenian personal income tax on worldwide income (earned in Slovenia and abroad), whereas a non-resident is taxed only on income sourced in Slovenia.
evidence_quote: Residents of Slovenia are liable to pay personal income tax only on all income earned in Slovenia and abroad, and non-residents are liable to pay personal income tax on income earned in Slovenia only.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Becoming Slovenian tax-resident pulls foreign income (investments, foreign rental, spouse-linked income) into Slovenian tax scope. Action: flag worldwide-income exposure and possible double-tax-treaty relief once residency flips.

entity_title: Employer, not employee, registers health insurance
fact_text: Compulsory health insurance with the Health Insurance Institute (ZZZS) is mandatory for employees, and it is the employer - not the worker - who is legally obliged to arrange the insurance registration.
evidence_quote: Employers are obliged by law to arrange registration, de-registration and changes to details on behalf of their workers.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Employees often expect to enrol themselves for health cover; in Slovenia the employer files the registration by law. Action: confirm the employer has filed the ZZZS registration at the start of the employment relationship.

entity_title: No compulsory cover means no access to services
fact_text: Access to publicly funded medical services and cash benefits in Slovenia is conditional on actually holding compulsory health insurance cover, so entitlement can be absent until the ZZZS registration is completed.
evidence_quote: you can exercise the right to medical services or cash benefits from compulsory health insurance only if you have compulsory health insurance cover.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Arriving in Slovenia does not itself grant healthcare access; entitlement starts only once compulsory cover is in place. Action: keep EHIC or private cover until ZZZS registration is confirmed to avoid an uninsured gap.

entity_title: EU/EEA work counts toward a Slovenian pension
fact_text: Insurance periods completed in other EU/EEA member states or Switzerland can be aggregated with Slovenian periods to satisfy the conditions for a pension, under Regulation (EC) No 883/2004, administered in Slovenia by ZPIZ.
evidence_quote: Regulation No 883/2004 allows persons who have been employed or insured in several Member States to meet the prescribed conditions for entitlement to a pension by aggregation of insurance periods.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Years paid into another EU/EEA scheme are not lost on moving to Slovenia; they count toward Slovenian pension eligibility via aggregation. Action: keep records of prior EU/EEA insurance periods for the eventual ZPIZ claim.

entity_title: Pro-rata pension, claimed where you live
fact_text: Where pension entitlement is met only by aggregating periods across member states, the pension is assessed on a pro-rata basis; a person residing in Slovenia lodges the claim at any ZPIZ regional unit or its Ljubljana headquarters.
evidence_quote: If the conditions for entitlement to a pension or other benefits are met solely by aggregating insurance periods completed in Member States, the pension is assessed on a pro-rata basis.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: A cross-border career yields several pro-rata pensions rather than one, and you file once in your country of residence. Action: lodge a single claim at ZPIZ if resident in Slovenia; it coordinates with the other member states.
